notes.title: Horizontal and vertical segments
notes.text: The gradient method in this example uses finite nonzero slopes. A horizontal segment has a vertical perpendicular bisector; a vertical segment has a horizontal one.

ican.text: I can find the midpoint of a segment from its endpoint coordinates.
I can find a perpendicular bisector from two points or from a line and a known midpoint.
I can handle horizontal and vertical segments without dividing by zero.
I can test whether a point lies on a perpendicular bisector using equal distances.
I can explain how a perpendicular bisector separates points nearer to one site from points nearer to the other.

ku.text: The perpendicular bisector of a segment passes through its midpoint and meets the segment at $90^\circ$. These are two separate conditions: a line satisfying only one is not necessarily the bisector.
For distinct endpoints $A(x_1,y_1)$ and $B(x_2,y_2)$, the midpoint is $M=(\frac{x_1+x_2}{2},\frac{y_1+y_2}{2})$.
When the original segment has finite nonzero gradient $m$, a perpendicular line has gradient $-1/m$. Find $m=(y_2-y_1)/(x_2-x_1)$, then use the midpoint in $y-y_M=m_\perp(x-x_M)$.

If the segment is horizontal, its bisector is the vertical line $x=x_M$. If the segment is vertical, its bisector is the horizontal line $y=y_M$. Vertical lines do not have a finite gradient, so the negative-reciprocal calculation does not apply directly.

If a segment’s line equation and midpoint are given, extract the segment direction from the equation, find a perpendicular direction and use the supplied midpoint. Confirm the stated midpoint lies on the stated line.

Every point on the perpendicular bisector is equally distant from the two endpoints. Conversely, a point equally distant from two distinct endpoints lies on their perpendicular bisector. This provides a second method: set the two squared distances equal and simplify.

The bisector divides the plane into two half-planes. Points on one side are closer to one endpoint; points on the other are closer to the other. To decide which, test a point or compare squared distances.
For more than two sites, a Voronoi edge is only the part of a pairwise bisector on which those sites are tied for nearest. Other sites may cut off part of the full line.
The endpoints must be distinct. If they coincide, there is no unique segment direction and every point is equally distant from the two identical locations.

misc.weak: The perpendicular bisector passes through endpoint $A$.
misc.better: It passes through the midpoint, which generally differs from either endpoint.

misc.weak: A line through the midpoint automatically bisects at a right angle.
misc.better: The line must also be perpendicular to the segment.

misc.weak: A vertical segment has a vertical perpendicular bisector.
Every point on a pairwise bisector is always a Voronoi edge.
misc.better: A third site may be closer. Only retain portions where the tied sites are nearest.

terms.text: An object that divides a segment or angle into two equal parts.
The point halfway along a segment; average corresponding endpoint coordinates.
The set of points satisfying a specified condition. Equal distance from two distinct fixed points defines their perpendicular bisector.
For a nonzero gradient $m$, the number $-1/m$.

formula.text: For a finite, nonzero segment gradient $m$, the perpendicular gradient is $-1/m$.
Point–slope form: $y-y_M=m_\perp(x-x_M)$. A vertical bisector instead has equation $x=x_M$.

worked.prompt: Two monitoring stations have coordinates $A=(2,-1)$ and $B=(8,3)$ on a plane map. One coordinate unit represents one kilometre.

parts.label: a
parts.q: Find the midpoint and the gradient of $AB$.

parts.label: b
parts.q: Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of $AB$.
parts.a: The perpendicular gradient is $-3/2$. Using $(5,1)$ gives $y-1=-\frac32(x-5)$, or $y=-\frac32x+\frac{17}{2}$. It passes through the midpoint and has a perpendicular direction.

parts.label: c
parts.q: Show that $P=(3,4)$ is equally far from the two stations.
parts.a: $PA^2=(3-2)^2+(4+1)^2=26$ and $PB^2=(3-8)^2+(4-3)^2=26$. Both distances are $\sqrt{26}$ km, so $P$ is equidistant; it also satisfies the line equation.

parts.label: d
parts.q: Determine which station is closer to $Q=(6,4)$.
parts.a: $QA^2=4^2+5^2=41$ and $QB^2=(-2)^2+1^2=5$. Since $5<41$, station $B$ is closer. Comparing squared distances is sufficient because distances are nonnegative.

parts.label: e
parts.q: A different segment lies on $2x-3y=-8$ and has midpoint $(-1,2)$. Find its perpendicular bisector.
parts.a: The midpoint satisfies $2(-1)-3(2)=-8$. Rearranging the segment line gives gradient $2/3$, so its perpendicular gradient is $-3/2$. Through $(-1,2)$ the bisector is $y-2=-\frac32(x+1)$, or $y=-\frac32x+\frac12$.

parts.label: f
parts.q: Find the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining $(1,4)$ and $(7,4)$.
parts.a: The midpoint is $(4,4)$ and the segment is horizontal, so its perpendicular bisector is the vertical line $x=4$.

kq.q: Why are points on the perpendicular bisector equally distant from the endpoints?
kq.model: The midpoint divides the segment into equal halves. The two right triangles formed with a point on the bisector share one leg and have equal other legs, so their hypotenuses are equal.

kq.q: Why is the midpoint used in point–slope form?
kq.model: It is a known point on the perpendicular bisector. An endpoint of the original segment is generally not on that line.

kq.q: Why can squared distances be compared instead of distances?
kq.model: Distances are nonnegative, and squaring preserves their order. The square root is unnecessary when deciding which is closer.

kq.q: Why might only part of a bisector appear on a Voronoi diagram?
kq.model: Another site may be closer along part of the bisector. A Voronoi edge keeps only locations where the tied sites are nearest.
